back: Improving answers by spending more compute at inference (more or longer samples, scorers, refinement) with the model weights unchanged.
Divide logits by T before the softmax: T<1 sharpens, T>1 flattens; T must be positive.
Sort probabilities descending, keep a token while the cumulative mass before it is < top_p (always keep the first), zero the rest, renormalise.
Sample n chains of thought, extract each final answer, return the most frequent one.
Plurality needs the largest count; majority needs more than half. Self-consistency is a plurality vote.
Return no answer (the book's rule), pick at random, or break ties with a scorer such as mean log-probability; each choice is a policy.
Score all n responses and keep the best. With a perfect verifier it equals pass@n; with a proxy scorer it inherits the scorer's errors.
A(n,p) = sum_{c>n/2} C(n,c) p^c (1-p)^(n-c) when wrong samples all give the same wrong answer.
With one wrong answer, voting helps iff p > 1/2 (to 1), hurts if p < 1/2 (to 0), stays at 1/2 at p = 1/2.
1 - A(n,p) <= exp(-2n(p-1/2)^2): exponential in n, controlled by the gap p - 1/2, but loose.

front: Why scattered wrong answers help voting
back: The correct answer only needs the largest count, so it can win with p < 1/2. Correlated, repeated mistakes remove that benefit.
In the book's CoT table accuracy per extra minute falls from about 0.107 to 0.024 to 0.0098 points/min as n goes 1 to 3 to 5 to 10.

A cap on generated tokens. Cutting a chain before its final box usually yields no extractable answer; budget forcing also extends short chains (general background, not implemented in the chapters read).

front: Why sampling n answers to one prompt batches well
back: All rows start from the same prompt length, so no padding is needed; throughput improves with batch size at the cost of memory (appendix E.5).
